Area.evidence_source: [/page/7/Text/5] Previous literature has identified that those bereaved by suicide may experience prolonged and intense grief (Cerel & Campbell, 2008; Cvinar, 2005; Mitchell et al., 2004) and so, when in contact with suicide survivors, nurses and other health care professionals need to be vigilant to the signs of complicated grief. A study by Dryregrov, Nordanger, and Dyregrov (2003), focusing on individual experiences of distress for those bereaved by suicide, found that those who had become socially isolated after bereavement had the highest levels of personal distress. Furthermore, their study noted a significantly higher level of distress for those who had been bereaved by an act of suicide or sudden accident, in comparison to people who had experienced a sudden infant death (SIDS). They note that an established survivor organisation for SIDS-related bereavement may be having a helpful impact on personal distress levels for family members. This further reinforces that nurses have an important role as facilitators of both formal and informal support pathways for suicide survivors. Formal assessment of survivors may be helpful in identifying those at high risk of suicide and[/page/7/Text/6] thus allow their timely referral to appropriate and supportive services.
